To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

penicillin binding-component I is the penicillin-sensitive transpeptidase, and that penicillin-binding component V is the D-alanine: carboxypeptide, and that the penicillin binding proteins of Bacillus subilis are localized in the cytoplasmic membrane.

the penicillin binding proteins of Bacillus subtlis are covalently linked to penicillin via an acyl-enzyme intermediate, that the peniciloyl moiety can be cleaved with neutral hydroxlyamine, and that penicillin binding protein V is a D-alanine carobxypeptidase.

the penicillin binding-components of B. subtilis can be isolated by a covalent affinity procedure, that penicillin binding-component 5 (the D-Alanine carboxypeptide) can be isolated from the membranes of B. subtlis with a 50% overall yield, and that the peniciloyl-enzyme linkage can be cleaved with neutral hydroxamine.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the isolation of membrane-bound proteins by affinity chromatography and the use of the purified enzymes in studies of membrane structure.
the development of a general technique for the isolation of membrane-bound proteins by their covalent attachment to a ligand.
the isolation of penicillin-binding proteins from Bacillus subtilus.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the method of covalent affinity is a very useful and versatile technique in protein chemistry.

the affinity chromatography procedure developed for the isolation of penicillin-binding component V from B. subtilis is simple, efficient, and rapid and is suitable for the purification of other enzymes which are bound covalently by penicillin.
the penicillin binding-component system of Bacillus subtitilis is not analogous to the penicillin-susceptibility system of Escherichia coli, although it does have some similarities.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
penicillin binding-component I is the penicillin binding protein of the cell wall.

the affinity chromatography technique described here is a useful method for the isolation of penicillin-binding proteins.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the penicillin binding components are present in the cell membrane in a form that can be solubilized in a single step by the detergent Nonide P-40 and that these proteins can be purified by a simple affinity chromatography procedure.
the technique of covalent affinity chromato- graphy can be used to isolate membrane-bound penicillin-binding proteins in pure form from membranes of gram-positive bacteria.
